title: Acute flaccid paralysis and Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with acute paralysis (onset over hours to days) in India: separating spinal cord from nerve, muscle and junction causes, recognising respiratory danger, and treating Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). Built on the ICMR Approach to Acute Paralysis workflow (October 2019) with the European Academy of Neurology/Peripheral Nerve Society (EAN/PNS) 2023 GBS guideline for diagnosis, respiratory thresholds and immunotherapy, and the enoxaparin label for clot prevention.
findings: Upper motor neuron (UMN) versus lower motor neuron (LMN) triage, causes by pattern, intubation triggers, referral destinations, admission and discharge criteria checked against the ICMR Acute Paralysis STW (October 2019).

GBS diagnostic features, modified Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (mEGRIS), forced vital capacity (FVC) thresholds, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) and plasma exchange regimens and timing, and recommendations against steroids and a second IVIg course taken from EAN/PNS 2023.
Enoxaparin prophylaxis dose from the US label.
unverifiedSections: Potassium replacement for hypokalaemic periodic paralysis was not dosed in an opened source; follow the local protocol and check serum potassium first (ICMR STW).
Gabapentin and carbamazepine for GBS pain are recommended by EAN/PNS (4.5.2) but no dose source was opened.
Steroid treatment for transverse myelitis is decided after magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at the referral centre; not dosed here.
Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in GBS is not addressed in the opened part of EAN/PNS; the enoxaparin row uses the label dose for immobile medical patients.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute paralysis is weakness of two or four limbs developing over hours to days. The ICMR workflow first separates upper motor neuron signs (spinal cord disease: trauma, tuberculosis, tumour, transverse myelitis, epidural abscess, cord infarct) from lower motor neuron signs (GBS, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, myasthenia gravis, snakebite, myopathy). GBS is an immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, often after diarrhoea or a respiratory infection, causing ascending symmetric weakness with absent reflexes that peaks within 4 weeks. The main early danger is respiratory and bulbar failure, so serial bedside breathing tests decide intubation (ICMR STW; EAN/PNS).
keyMechanisms: In GBS, antibodies raised against an infection cross-react with nerve myelin or axons (molecular mimicry).
Demyelination or axonal damage blocks conduction, causing flaccid weakness and lost reflexes.
Phrenic, intercostal and bulbar nerve involvement causes respiratory failure and aspiration.
Autonomic nerve involvement causes swings in blood pressure and heart rate.

symptoms: Weakness of legs or all four limbs over hours to days (ICMR STW)
Tingling and limb or back pain (EAN/PNS supportive features)
Difficulty swallowing, choking on water, breathlessness (ICMR STW admission criteria)
Recent diarrhoea, respiratory infection or fever within 6 weeks (EAN/PNS)
physicalSigns: LMN pattern: reduced or absent reflexes, wasting, sensory impairment (ICMR STW)
UMN pattern: brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, increased tone, sensory level, bladder or bowel incontinence (ICMR STW)
Fatigable weakness or eye-movement weakness: myasthenia or snakebite (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Unable to complete sentences, low or falling single breath count, short breath-holding time, poor chest expansion: intubate (ICMR STW)
Respiratory rate above 20/min or SaO2 below 95% (ICMR STW admission)
FVC below 20 mL/kg: consider elective ventilation; below 10 mL/kg: intubation almost inevitable (EAN/PNS)
Persistent heart rate above 100/min; bowel or bladder involvement; fever (ICMR STW)
Inability to cough, inability to lift arms above horizontal, neck flexion weakness (EAN/PNS respiratory risk)
precipitants: Diarrhoeal or respiratory infection within 6 weeks (EAN/PNS)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Sensory level, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, early bladder involvement; needs urgent MRI (ICMR STW).
Recurrent episodes, no sensory loss, low serum potassium (ICMR STW).
Fatigable weakness with ptosis or eye-movement weakness; normal sensation (ICMR STW).
Bite history, ptosis and bulbar weakness (ICMR STW).
Proximal weakness, no sensory loss, raised creatine kinase (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Progressive weakness of arms and legs; absent or reduced reflexes in weak limbs; progression for no more than 4 weeks.
Persistent asymmetric weakness, fever at onset, sensory level, extensor plantars, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) above 50 cells/µL.

mEGRIS 0–17 low (under 20%), 18–24 moderate, 25–32 high (over 70%). FVC under 60% predicted, aspiration risk or autonomic instability: intensive care unit (ICU) assessment. Single breath count under 20: consider ICU.
Progressive weakness, unable to walk, unable to swallow, respiratory distress, heart rate above 100/min, fever, or bowel or bladder involvement.
Cause established; weakness no longer progressing; breathing unaided; carers trained in tracheostomy, tube feeding, catheter care, turning and home physiotherapy as needed.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Do early; a normal first-week study does not exclude GBS, repeat if needed (EAN/PNS 4.2.8); ICMR STW refers for these tests.

clinicalManagement.title: Triage at first contact
actions: Pulse, blood pressure and respiration (ICMR STW).
Separate UMN from LMN signs; check serum potassium in LMN pattern (ICMR STW).
Intubate if unable to complete sentences, single breath count low, breath-holding time low or chest expansion poor (ICMR STW).
UMN signs: catheterise for retention and refer to a centre with MRI (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Referral
actions: Suspected GBS with absent reflexes: refer to a district hospital or medical college with plasma exchange or IVIg and a ventilator (ICMR STW).
Myasthenia or snakebite: same intubation criteria; refer for nerve conduction studies, plasma exchange or IVIg and ventilation (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Respiratory and autonomic monitoring
actions: Score mEGRIS on admission; serial FVC if available (EAN/PNS).
ICU assessment for FVC under 60% predicted, aspiration risk or autonomic instability; immediate ICU transfer if FVC falls over 30% in 24 hours (EAN/PNS).

clinicalManagement.title: Immunotherapy for GBS
actions: Unable to walk unaided: IVIg within 2 weeks of onset, or plasma exchange within 4 weeks (EAN/PNS 4.3.5, 4.3.8).
Do not give plasma exchange followed straight by IVIg, a routine second IVIg course, or corticosteroids (EAN/PNS 4.3.8, 4.3.10, 4.3.13).

clinicalManagement.title: Supportive care and rehabilitation
actions: Clot prevention while immobile; turning; catheter and feeding care (ICMR STW discharge teaching).
Physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy from the acute phase; continue beyond 6 months if needed (EAN/PNS 4.4.2).
Pain: gabapentinoid or tricyclic, with caution in autonomic failure (EAN/PNS 4.5).

regimens.duration: 5 days; start within 2 weeks of onset
adjustments: Paediatric: Same weight-based dose used in children; seek paediatric neurology advice.
Penicillin allergy: Not an antibiotic; penicillin allergy does not change this medicine.
CKD: Check creatinine and hydrate; kidney injury risk with some products.
CLD: Not specified in the cited sources; check the formulary.
contraindications: Selective IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies; recent thrombosis

medicationPlan.note: ICMR STW gives triage and referral but no drug doses; IVIg and plasma exchange regimens follow EAN/PNS 2023, and clot prevention the enoxaparin label. Corticosteroids are not recommended for GBS (EAN/PNS). Other causes (myelitis, hypokalaemia, myasthenia, snakebite) follow their own pathways. Not clinically reviewed.

teaching.scope: Adult acute flaccid paralysis and GBS.
learningObjectives: Separate UMN from LMN acute paralysis.
Choose and time immunotherapy in GBS.
keyPoints: Check potassium in every LMN paralysis.
Single breath count and chest expansion decide intubation.
IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days within 2 weeks, or plasma exchange within 4 weeks.
pitfalls: Waiting for respiratory distress before referring.
Missing a cord lesion with a sensory level.
Plasma exchange immediately followed by IVIg.

patientEducation: Most people with GBS improve over weeks to months; recovery can continue beyond a year.
Report any new breathlessness, choking or palpitations at once.
lifestyleAndDiet: Safe swallowing or tube feeding as assessed
mdtReferrals: Psychological support for patient and carers (EAN/PNS)
dischargeCriteria: Carers trained in catheter care, turning and home physiotherapy (ICMR STW)
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow up at the community health centre for medicines and rehabilitation (ICMR STW); continue rehabilitation beyond 6 months if limitations persist (EAN/PNS).
